approach_variants.name: Reynolds Creek Trail and the South Fork drainage
approach_variants.notes: The short way in, and short is relative. From the road end off the Twisp River an unmaintained primitive trail climbs through forest alongside the creek for roughly three miles. Above the confluence the tread gives out and about two miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder, downed timber and a boot path that comes and goes is the real crux of the day — several parties lose more time here than on the mountain. The basin above holds snow well into summer, so an axe is worth carrying even when the valley looks dry. Mark the point where you leave the tread; it is easy to miss coming down.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September; axe for snow
hazards: About two miles of intermittent bushwhack above the confluence through slide alder and downed timber, with a boot path that comes and goes
Deadfall and heavy brush on the lower unmaintained trail
Avalanche terrain on the approach slopes and summit gully whenever they hold snow
Loose rock and real exposure on the summit block
Breakable crust and postholing on spring ascents
Afternoon thunderstorms on this dry east-side peak
approach_variants.baseFinding: Follow the creek trail to about 4,800 ft, where the forest opens at the confluence of the South Fork with the main creek — a real, obvious junction of two running streams, usually crossed on a downed log. That confluence is where you leave the maintained tread. Follow the South Fork drainage upward staying roughly fifty feet above the water, which keeps you out of the worst alder and log-hopping in the streambed itself. Timber thins around 5,600 ft and the drainage narrows into a ravine that opens into a broad talus and scree basin directly beneath the peak's southeast face; that basin, at roughly 5,500 to 6,700 ft depending where you stop, is the base of the climbing. From it, a gully that often holds snow well into summer leads up to a notch on the ridge above. The decoy is at the top rather than the bottom: two horns stand across a short notch, the northern one is reached first and is lower, and the true summit is the southern horn.

approach_variants.name: Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge

approachLogistics.trailhead: Williams Creek Trailhead (West Twisp River Road)

approach_variants.notes: Longer, but on good trail at first and far more scenic. From the Williams Creek trailhead on the West Twisp River road at about 2,800 ft, follow the well-marked trail to Williams Lake at about 6,500 ft, then climb over Williams Butte and follow War Creek Ridge toward Camel's Hump. Drop through a boulder break in the cliffs into the upper South Fork Reynolds Creek basin and climb heather and scree to the summit pyramid. It can be strung into a loop with a neighbouring summit, and it joins the same finish as the Reynolds Creek way.
hazards: Longer day with big elevation gain via Williams Lake and over Williams Butte and War Creek Ridge
Drop through a cliff-band boulder break into the upper South Fork basin; route-finding needed
Avalanche terrain on the summit gully whenever it holds snow
Loose rock and talus on the upper gully and Class 3-4 summit block
Lingering snow in the summit gully through early summer
Afternoon thunderstorms on this dry east-side peak
approach_variants.whyThisWay: When you want a longer, scenic outing on good trail instead of the brushy creek bushwhack, or an overnight or loop with a neighbouring summit, camping at the lake.

waypoints.name: Reynolds Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Spur 4435-015 off FR 4435, which turns off Twisp River Road (~18.3 mi from Twisp); a self-issue wilderness permit is typical at the kiosk, but no Northwest Forest Pass is required at this unimproved trailhead.
waypoints.directions: From Twisp, drive west up the Twisp River Road (FR 44) for 18.3 miles and bear left onto FR 4435. Cross the Twisp River in 0.3 mile, turn right after the bridge to stay on FR 4435, drive 1.1 miles upriver and turn left onto Spur 4435-015, reaching the trailhead in another 0.3 mile at about 3,100 ft. A free self-issued Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness permit is filled out at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: South Fork Reynolds Creek confluence
waypoints.note: Trail opens up where the South Fork joins the Main Fork; cross on a log and leave the trail here and stay on one side of the South Fork, above the streambed, to avoid extra creek crossings and heavy log-hopping.
waypoints.directions: Follow Reynolds Creek Trail #402 up the north side of Reynolds Creek through forest for about 2.8 miles to around 4,800 ft, where the South Fork valley comes in from the south. The trail is primitive and sees little maintenance, so expect deadfall.

waypoints.name: Upper Reynolds Creek basin
waypoints.note: Open basin below Reynolds' east face where trees give way to scree and talus; last flat ground and reliable creek water before the summit push.
waypoints.directions: Cross the creek on a downed log at the confluence and leave the maintained tread. Follow the South Fork drainage upward, staying roughly 50 ft above the water to avoid the worst alder and log-hopping, for about 2 miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder and downed timber on a boot path that comes and goes. The timber thins around 5,600 ft and a ravine opens into the talus and scree basin below the southeast face.

waypoints.name: Reynolds-Rennie saddle
waypoints.note: Unnamed saddle/ridge crest between Reynolds and the Rennie/Camel's Hump massif; loose sand, scree and talus underfoot on the final approach to it.
waypoints.directions: Climb scree, talus and, early in the season, snow up the gully out of the basin to the saddle on the ridge above. The gully often holds snow well into summer; carry an axe.

waypoints.name: Summit block gully
waypoints.note: Class 3-4 gully splits the summit block to a notch in the ridge crest; loose, sometimes snow-covered rock with real exposure — the crux of the standard route.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle, move into the loose gully that splits the summit block and climb it toward the notch in the crest. This is the Class 3-4 crux, with real exposure and rock that is sometimes snow-covered.

waypoints.name: Reynolds Peak (true/south summit)
waypoints.note: True summit is the south horn; the lower North Peak (8,384 ft) sits about 0.3 mi north across the notch.
waypoints.directions: Scramble the exposed summit rocks to the true summit, the southern of the two horns. The lower north peak across the notch is not the high point.

before.name: Standard Scramble
before.fa: A USGS survey party including Albert H. Sylvester, 1898 or 1899 (first ascent of the peak)
gear: Ice axe and crampons for snow-covered approaches (spring, early summer, and winter ascents)
Trekking poles for off-trail travel in the South Fork Reynolds Creek basin
Skis with skins and ski crampons for winter ski-mountaineering ascents, plus crampons/axe for the final gully
hazards: Avalanche terrain on the approach slopes and summit gully — explicitly flagged for this route and confirmed by old avalanche debris found in the summit gully after a January storm during a documented winter ascent
Loose rock/talus on the Class 3-4 south summit block
Deadfall and brush on the lower Reynolds Creek Trail from infrequent maintenance
Afternoon thunderstorms common in summer on this dry, east-side Cascades peak
Breakable snow crust and postholing on spring ascents/descents
before.overview: Reynolds Peak (8,517 ft) is a high, horned, twin-summited peak on the divide between the Twisp River and Lake Chelan country, within the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness (Methow Mountains, North Cascades), about 6 miles northeast of Stehekin. It is one of the most visually striking summits in the Chelan Sawtooth range even though it isn't the highest. The south summit is the true high point; a subsidiary North Peak (8,384 ft) sits 0.3 mile to the north and is easy to mistake for the top since it's reached first and is non-technical. Rock is a sound tonalitic orthogneiss. Isolation to the nearest higher peak (Oval Peak) is about 8.5 miles, and local relief above Reynolds Creek exceeds 3,500 ft within a mile, giving the peak its prominent, rugged look from the Twisp River valley.
before.beta: Parties typically approach via Twisp River Road to either the Reynolds Creek drainage (shortest, most direct) or the Williams Creek trail, then climb open basins and snowfields on the southeast side of the peak to a saddle/notch below the summit. From there, a Class 2-3 gully leads to the ridge crest, followed by a short, somewhat exposed Class 3 scramble on solid granite to the true (southeast) summit. Longer alternative approaches traverse in from Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge, or from the west via Bridge Creek and Stehekin ('the back way'), but all eventually join the same southeast-side summit scramble rather than offering a genuinely distinct technical line.
before.turnaround: Turn around before entering the summit gully or the exposed notch section if it is snow- or ice-covered beyond your party's comfort with an ice axe, if visibility drops (route-finding through the talus and gendarmes is difficult in a whiteout), or if afternoon thunderstorms are building, since the upper ridge offers little shelter.
before.permit: Free self-issue Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. No parking pass is needed at the Reynolds Creek Trailhead.
obj_haz: Loose rock and talus on the upper gully and summit notch
Exposed Class 3 scrambling on the ridge just below the summit
Lingering snow/ice in the summit gully through early summer
Wildfire closures have affected the standard eastern approach in past seasons

before.detailed_rack: Not a technical rock climb — most parties solo the Class 2-3 terrain, but a short (30m) rope with a few slings/runners is worth carrying to protect the exposed Class 3 step below the summit with a running belay.
what_to_bring: microspikes/light crampons — consider in early season for the snow gully and approach snowfields
Ice axe (early June, for the basin snow and summit-block approach)
pro_tips: Good glissading on the descent when snow is present on the upper slopes
Check current trail conditions before committing — the Reynolds Creek Trail has gone multiple seasons without a chainsaw/brushing crew, leading to significant deadfall
The South Fork Reynolds Creek basin variant (SE snowfield to the east ridge) gives an easier, more consistent Class 2-3 finish than the direct saddle line
Also climbed as a winter ski-mountaineering objective via the SE basin and a narrowing summit gully — expect mixed 4th-class rock/snow near the top and check for avalanche debris after storms.
A snow-free flat camp exists on a prominence near 6,700-6,800 ft in the basin by early June, and water there is abundant while snow lasts.
watch_out: Don't mistake the North Peak (8,384 ft, reached first, non-technical) for the true summit — the higher south summit is 0.3 mile further and requires Class 3-4 scrambling
Loose rock and exposure on the summit block
Avalanche-prone gullies and slopes when snow-covered
Early-June glissade down the basin: soft snow over buried rock and small trees punches through (Jun).
before.pro_needs: Unroped class 2-3 scramble; no technical gear normally required.
before.best_season: Mid-July through September for a dry Class 3-4 scramble on the true (south) summit block; also climbed as a snow route April-June via the SE basin and gullies (ice axe/crampons), and as a winter ski-mountaineering objective (documented ascent via Twisp River Sno-Park by snowmobile/ski, Jan 2021).
before.approach: From the Reynolds Creek Trailhead (~3,100–3,170 ft, reached via Forest Road 4435, which crosses the Twisp River near Mystery Campground before the Spur 4435-015 turnoff to the trailhead), the route follows Reynolds Creek Trail #402, an unmaintained, primitive Forest Service trail entering the Lake Chelan–Sawtooth Wilderness. Trail #402 climbs steadily through mixed conifer forest along Reynolds Creek for roughly 3 miles to the confluence where the South Fork of Reynolds Creek meets the main creek (approx. 4,800–5,000 ft) — parties describe scooting across a downed log to make this crossing, which can be a genuine ford in high early-season flow. This confluence is the last reliable, easy water source before the upper basin, so fill up here. Beyond the crossing, leave the maintained tread and follow the South Fork drainage, staying roughly 50 ft above the creek to avoid the worst brush and log-hopping directly in the streambed. Expect about 2 miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder, downed timber, and a boot-path/game-trail tread that comes and goes — this is the route-finding crux of the approach, and parties specifically flag the numerous fallen logs and dense brush here. The drainage opens into a broad talus/scree basin around 5,500–5,700 ft directly below Reynolds Peak's southeast face and the gully/snowfield leading to its east ridge. This basin and the gully above it hold snow well into summer in most years, so carry an ice axe (and traction in early season) even on an otherwise dry-looking late-summer day. From the basin, ascend the scree, talus, and (seasonally) snow of the SE slopes/gully to a saddle/notch on the peak's east ridge, then finish with a short, exposed class 2–3 scramble (occasionally reported as harder, class 3–4, depending on snow coverage) up sound granite summit rocks to the 8,517 ft high point. An alternate, more scenic but similarly long approach exists via Williams Creek Trail and War Creek Ridge from a different Twisp River Road trailhead, but Reynolds Creek Trail #402 is the standard, shorter line. The longer Williams Creek/War Creek Ridge alternative can be combined into a loop with Abernathy Peak or Twisp Pass, running roughly 24 miles round trip with about 8,300 ft of cumulative gain.
before.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line — there is no rappelling on the standard route. Downclimb the class 2–3 summit rocks back to the saddle/notch on the east ridge, then descend the scree, talus, and snow gully back into the SE basin at ~5,500–5,700 ft. When the gully still holds good snow (common well into summer), this section glissades or plunge-steps quickly; once it melts out to bare scree/talus later in the season it becomes a slower, loose descent — go one at a time through any group to avoid knocking rock onto climbers below. From the basin, pick up the boot path along the South Fork's climber's-right bank back to the log crossing at the South Fork/main Reynolds Creek confluence (~4,800–5,000 ft), then follow Reynolds Creek Trail #402 the remaining ~3 miles of forest trail back to the Reynolds Creek Trailhead. This is a full retrace/walk-off descent with no fixed anchors or rappel stations reported anywhere on the standard route; treat any exposed class 3 downclimbing on the summit rocks with care rather than as a rappel substitute.
before.bail: Retreat down the ascent slopes to camp.

itinerary.cal: Steep upper snow/rock bands can hold snow into early-mid summer, so an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) is commonly carried even on this 'scramble.'

days.note: This is a long but standard single-day scramble, not a backpack trip. From the Reynolds Creek Trailhead, follow the trail about 3 miles, leave it at about 4,800 ft where the South Fork comes in and cross Reynolds Creek, then climb through a basin and steep snow/rock bands to class 3-4 terrain on the summit ridge. Most fit parties treat it as an 11-13 hour car-to-car day.
days.title: Car-to-car summit day

schedule.label: Leave trailhead
schedule.detail: Reynolds Creek Trailhead, ~3,170 ft; an early start is recommended so the long day doesn't finish after dark.

schedule.label: Leave maintained trail
schedule.detail: At about 4,800 ft, where the South Fork joins, leave the Reynolds Creek Trail and cross the creek on a log, then contour toward the upper basin.

schedule.label: Enter the upper basin
schedule.detail: Ascend steep snow and negotiate minor rock bands toward the east face below the summit block.

schedule.label: Class 3-4 scramble to summit ridge
schedule.detail: Climb steep snow or class 4 rock to gain the ridge, then follow mostly snow-free class 3 rock to the true (south) summit.

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: South summit, 8,517 ft; the lower north summit (8,384 ft) is a short distance away.

schedule.label: Back at trailhead
schedule.detail: Reverse the ascent line, downclimbing the rock bands carefully; a Mountaineers party finishing an 8 AM start returned at 9:15 PM (13 hr day).

days.objective: Reach the 8,517 ft south summit of Reynolds Peak and return to the Reynolds Creek Trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A long, strenuous single day: about 11 miles round trip with roughly 5,400 ft of gain/loss, typically 11-13 hours car-to-car from the Reynolds Creek Trailhead.

access.fees: No fee or pass is required at the Reynolds Creek Trailhead
access.rules: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness: max group size 12 people/18 head of stock, no motorized or mechanized equipment, proper bear-resistant food storage required, don't tie/graze stock within 200 ft of lakeshores, pack out all waste
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit typical at Okanogan-Wenatchee NF wilderness trailheads; the reservation-based North Cascades NP/Lake Chelan NRA backcountry permit system does not apply to this Twisp-side approach
access.closures: Twisp River Road and the FR 4435/Spur 4435-015 trailhead spur are not plowed in winter; winter and ski-mountaineering parties have accessed via Twisp River Sno-Park by snowmobile or ski
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District (within the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness)

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead registration box. No parking pass is needed at this trailhead.

road.name: Twisp River Road (to FR 4435 / Spur 4435-015)
road.status: Gravel/dirt, generally passable to a passenger car in summer; the final spur may be rougher
road.driveNote: From Twisp, 18.3 miles west on Twisp River Road, left across the river on FR 4435 for 1.1 miles, then left on Spur 4435-015 for 0.3 mile to the Reynolds Creek Trailhead (3,170 ft)
road.seasonalGate: Not maintained in winter beyond the lower Twisp River Road corridor; roughly closed by snow November-April

climate.typical: Warm, often dry summer days with a real risk of afternoon thunderstorms; being on the dry, east side of the Cascade crest, it sees less precipitation than peaks further west, but snow can linger on the upper mountain into early summer and return by early fall

bySeason.fall: Early snow possible by late September/October, especially on north-facing terrain
bySeason.spring: Snow climb conditions on the upper slopes and gullies; avalanche hazard and postholing are real concerns
bySeason.summer: Primary Class 3-4 scrambling season; watch for afternoon thunderstorms
bySeason.winter: Ski-mountaineering objective for experienced parties; road access requires snowmobile or ski approach from Twisp River Sno-Park, and the summit gully can hold avalanche debris and icy slab

emergency.notes: Aero Methow Rescue Service (based in the Methow Valley) provides local emergency medical response/transport for the Twisp/Winthrop area; for backcountry rescue, dial 911 and expect Okanogan County Sheriff SAR to coordinate on the Twisp River Road side
emergency.county: Chelan County (summit); the standard Twisp River Road approach is from Okanogan County
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest; Forest Supervisor's Office: 215 Melody Lane, Wenatchee, WA 98801, (509) 664-9200
emergency.nearestHospital: Three Rivers Hospital, Brewster, WA — the nearest full-service hospital to the Twisp River Road trailheads

crowds.peakTraffic: summer weekends, July-August, mostly WA prominence/"Bulger" peak-baggers and Mountaineers-affiliated scramble parties rather than casual hikers
crowds.estimatePerSeason: roughly 10-25 parties per season (rough estimate from recurring trip reports, not an official count)

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very strong - about 11 miles round trip with roughly 5,400 ft of gain, normally done as a single long day car-to-car rather than backpacked over multiple days
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light daypack (approx. 15-20 lb) for the single-day car-to-car push; add ice axe/crampons weight in early-season snow conditions

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long single-day push - typically 11-13 hours car-to-car from the Reynolds Creek Trailhead; not a multi-day backpack
requiredSkills: endurance for a long, strenuous single-day car-to-car push
comfort operating with limited-to-no cell coverage far from help
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Solid off-trail scrambler comfortable with loose talus, exposed Class 2-3 terrain, and a long, strenuous single-day car-to-car push; not a beginner objective given the long, mostly unmaintained approach

July.reason: Conditions improve through the month; best season begins mid-July, so early July can still carry residual snow and high runoff

June.reason: Snow can still linger on the crest and approach; creek crossings on War Creek/Reynolds Creek run high with snowmelt. In early June the creek basin still carries firm snow from roughly 5,800 ft up, the summit block itself can already be bare, and meltwater is plentiful; a glissade back to camp is possible but the thin snow punches through beside rocks.

August.reason: Most reliable dry conditions and stable access; watch for typical afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed crest

September.reason: Generally stable weather but shorter daylight; early-season snow is possible late in the month

weather.typical: East-Cascades continental pattern - warm, dry summer days with cold nights at elevation and limited water along the crest
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are common in July-August on the exposed summit ridge

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Primary hazard is loose talus/blocky granite on Class 2-3 terrain rather than sustained technical exposure; consequences of a slip or injury are amplified by the long, remote approach and lack of cell coverage

avalanche.zone: N/A for the standard dry-season Class 2-3 scramble; however a documented winter ascent variant exists that crosses real avalanche terrain (old debris confirmed in the summit gully after a January storm) — check the Okanogan NWAC zone before any winter/early-season attempt

gaps: Current (2026) status of trailhead fee/pass requirements and Reynolds Creek Trail #402 maintenance/deadfall should be reconfirmed before a trip
Exact snow/avalanche route conditions vary significantly year to year and season to season on the summit gully
GPS track sourced from public CalTopo map: https://caltopo.com/m/GGSG

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Reynolds Creek Trailhead (~3,100-3,170 ft, reached via Forest Road 4435, which crosses the Twisp River near Mystery Campground before the Spur 4435-015 turnoff to the trailhead), the route follows Reynolds Creek Trail #402, an unmaintained, primitive Forest Service trail entering the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness.

before.rope_note: Class 3-4 scramble, non-technical except a few hundred feet of 3rd/4th class near the true (South) summit; no rope used in standard dry-condition ascents.
before.corrections: Grade/terrain-based inference; avalanche-exposed slopes noted for early-season snow.

approach_variants.name: Reynolds Creek Trail and the South Fork drainage
approach_variants.notes: The short way in, and short is relative. From the road end off the Twisp River an unmaintained primitive trail climbs through forest alongside the creek for roughly three miles. Above the confluence the tread gives out and about two miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder, downed timber and a boot path that comes and goes is the real crux of the day — several parties lose more time here than on the mountain. The basin above holds snow well into summer, so an axe is worth carrying even when the valley looks dry. Mark the point where you leave the tread; it is easy to miss coming down.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September; axe for snow
hazards: About two miles of intermittent bushwhack above the confluence through slide alder and downed timber, with a boot path that comes and goes
Deadfall and heavy brush on the lower unmaintained trail
Avalanche terrain on the approach slopes and summit gully whenever they hold snow
Loose rock and real exposure on the summit block
Breakable crust and postholing on spring ascents
Afternoon thunderstorms on this dry east-side peak
approach_variants.baseFinding: Follow the creek trail to about 4,800 ft, where the forest opens at the confluence of the South Fork with the main creek — a real, obvious junction of two running streams, usually crossed on a downed log. That confluence is where you leave the maintained tread. Follow the South Fork drainage upward staying roughly fifty feet above the water, which keeps you out of the worst alder and log-hopping in the streambed itself. Timber thins around 5,600 ft and the drainage narrows into a ravine that opens into a broad talus and scree basin directly beneath the peak's southeast face; that basin, at roughly 5,500 to 6,700 ft depending where you stop, is the base of the climbing. From it, a gully that often holds snow well into summer leads up to a notch on the ridge above. The decoy is at the top rather than the bottom: two horns stand across a short notch, the northern one is reached first and is lower, and the true summit is the southern horn.

approach_variants.name: Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge

approachLogistics.trailhead: Williams Creek Trailhead (West Twisp River Road)

approach_variants.notes: Longer, but on good trail at first and far more scenic. From the Williams Creek trailhead on the West Twisp River road at about 2,800 ft, follow the well-marked trail to Williams Lake at about 6,500 ft, then climb over Williams Butte and follow War Creek Ridge toward Camel's Hump. Drop through a boulder break in the cliffs into the upper South Fork Reynolds Creek basin and climb heather and scree to the summit pyramid. It can be strung into a loop with a neighbouring summit, and it joins the same finish as the Reynolds Creek way.
hazards: Longer day with big elevation gain via Williams Lake and over Williams Butte and War Creek Ridge
Drop through a cliff-band boulder break into the upper South Fork basin; route-finding needed
Avalanche terrain on the summit gully whenever it holds snow
Loose rock and talus on the upper gully and Class 3-4 summit block
Lingering snow in the summit gully through early summer
Afternoon thunderstorms on this dry east-side peak
approach_variants.whyThisWay: When you want a longer, scenic outing on good trail instead of the brushy creek bushwhack, or an overnight or loop with a neighbouring summit, camping at the lake.

climbing_route.label: SE slopes/gully to the east ridge notch
climbing_route.notes: From the talus/scree basin at 5,500-5,700 ft directly below Reynolds Peak's southeast face, ascend the scree, talus, and (seasonally) snow of the SE slopes/gully to a saddle/notch on the peak's east ridge. This basin and the gully above it hold snow well into summer in most years, so carry an ice axe and traction in early season even on an otherwise dry-looking late-summer day.

climbing_route.label: Summit rocks from the notch
climbing_route.notes: A short, exposed class 2-3 scramble, occasionally reported as harder (class 3-4) depending on snow coverage, up sound granite summit rocks to the 8,517 ft high point.

bivy.name: Reynolds Creek upper basin
bivy.notes: The obvious camp for the Reynolds Peak scramble, and it turns an 11-mile day with 5,300 ft of gain into a comfortable two. Access is easy to get wrong: drive the Twisp River road about 19 miles to Mystery Campground, cross the river there on the forest road, and follow it a little over a mile to a junction and then to the Reynolds Creek trailhead at around 3,100 ft. Mystery Campground itself is the fallback if you arrive late and want a roadside night before starting. Follow the Reynolds Creek trail on the north side of the creek to somewhere above 4,800 ft, where a log crossing puts you into the basin. Camp there, with water and views, and the summit is then a scree and talus grind to a short easy scramble through the summit rocks. Snow lingers in the upper basin later than the sunny Sawtooth crest to the south because this side faces roughly north, so early July trips should expect snow on the approach slopes. The valley has burned in places in recent seasons and blowdown on the lower trail is a recurring nuisance; check the current trail report rather than assuming a clean tread.
bivy.water: Reynolds Creek runs through the basin and is the reason to camp here rather than higher. Filter it. Above the basin the slopes are dry talus and scree with nothing until you are back down.
bivy.permit: Forest Service ground, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the trailhead. Stove only in practice - fires are usually restricted here through the dry months and there is little to burn.
bivy.capacity: Informal sites in the upper basin, a handful of parties at most. No numbered sites, no toilet, nothing built.
